stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: A study of hand-washing stations at rural primary schools found that absences from diarrheal illness fell by nearly a third once soap was kept stocked. The study's lead author, epidemiologist Mariam Osei of the Accra Public Health ______ argued that the cheapest part of the intervention, the soap itself, was also the part most often neglected.
explanation: A comma after "author" opens the extra phrase that names her, "epidemiologist Mariam Osei of the Accra Public Health Institute." You close that phrase with a matching comma. Cross the phrase out and the sentence still reads correctly: "The study's lead author argued that..."

B.why: You left the interrupter open. The comma after "author" needs a closing comma, or else the phrase runs straight into "argued" and is never fenced off from the main sentence.

C.why: You put a semicolon after a fragment. "The study's lead author, epidemiologist Mariam Osei..." has no verb yet, so it can't stand alone, and a semicolon needs a complete sentence on both sides.

D.why: You added "and" as if two actions were being joined. The subject "author" has no earlier verb, so "and argued" leaves the sentence without a main verb.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Farmers in the American Midwest have long left fields bare over the winter, but that practice is changing. Cover crops—plants such as clover and winter rye that are grown between cash-crop ______ can hold topsoil in place through spring storms and return nitrogen to the ground when they decompose.
explanation: A dash after "Cover crops" opens the description of what cover crops are. An interruption has to be closed with the same mark that opened it, so you need a second dash after "seasons." Remove the fenced-off part and you get "Cover crops can hold topsoil in place...", which is a complete, correct sentence.

B.why: You closed a dash interruption with a comma. The marks around an interrupter have to match, and this one opened with a dash.

C.why: You left the interrupter unclosed. Without a second dash, the inserted description never ends and runs straight into the main verb, "can hold."

D.why: You used a semicolon after a fragment. "Cover crops—plants such as clover..." has no main verb yet, so it can't stand on its own as a sentence.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Most salamanders lose their gills as they mature and move onto land. The axolotl, a salamander that keeps its feathery external gills throughout ______ in the wild only in a handful of canals near Mexico City, where pollution and introduced fish have pushed its numbers sharply downward.
explanation: The comma after "axolotl" opens an appositive that describes the animal. The appositive ends at "adulthood," so you need a closing comma there before the main verb, "survives." Cross out the appositive and you have "The axolotl survives in the wild only in a handful of canals..."

B.why: You left the appositive unclosed. Because the comma after "axolotl" opened it, a comma has to close it before "survives."

C.why: You put a semicolon between a subject and its verb. The words before the semicolon form a fragment with no main verb, so they can't stand alone.

D.why: You used a colon after a fragment. A colon needs a complete sentence before it, and "The axolotl, a salamander that..." doesn't have its verb yet.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Before 1781, astronomers recognized only the six planets visible to the unaided eye. That March, William Herschel, a German-born musician who ground his own telescope mirrors in Bath, ______ a faint, slowly moving object that he first took to be a comet. It turned out to be Uranus, the first planet discovered with a telescope.
explanation: The comma after "Herschel" opens a phrase describing him, and that phrase ends at "Bath, England." You close it with a matching comma. Without the interrupter the sentence reads "That March, William Herschel spotted a faint, slowly moving object..."

B.why: You left the descriptive phrase open. The comma after "Herschel" needs a partner before the main verb, "spotted."

C.why: You added "and" as if two actions were being joined. "Herschel" has no verb before "and," so the sentence ends up with no main verb.

D.why: You closed the interrupter with a dash after opening it with a comma. The marks have to match at both ends.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Every flat map of the globe distorts something: area, distance, shape, or direction. Gerardus Mercator, the Flemish cartographer whose 1569 world map drew lines of constant compass bearing as straight ______ is still blamed for making Greenland look nearly as large as Africa, even though navigators valued his projection for exactly that trade-off.
explanation: The comma after "Mercator" opens an appositive that identifies him. The appositive ends at "straight lines," so you close it with a comma there. Take it out and you have "Gerardus Mercator is still blamed for making Greenland look nearly as large as Africa..."

B.why: You left the appositive unclosed. It opened with a comma after "Mercator," so it needs a closing comma before the main verb, "is."

C.why: You used a semicolon after a fragment. "Gerardus Mercator, the Flemish cartographer whose..." has no main verb, so it can't stand alone.

D.why: You added "and" as if a second action were being joined to a first one. "Mercator" has no verb before "and," so the sentence is left without a main verb.
